Chapter 6. Turning Conversations into Growth—The Art of Individualized Coaching.
Now that we’ve built a strong foundation for engagement, what’s the next step? It’s all about turning our daily conversations into real opportunities for growth.
The most effective managers don’t just wait for those once-a-year reviews to talk about performance or development. Instead, they make coaching a natural part of everyday work. Every conversation—whether it’s a quick check-in or a focused discussion—can help someone move forward.
Think of it like tending a campfire. If you give it small, steady attention, the flame stays strong. But if you only throw on fuel every now and then, that fire can sputter out or burn too hot. The best managers use regular one-on-ones to check in on progress, talk about roadblocks, and listen to what their team members really want to achieve. Each conversation is shaped around the individual—focusing on their unique strengths, their goals, and what matters most to them.
So, how do you put individualized coaching into practice? Here are a few simple, powerful techniques.
First, ask open-ended questions. Instead of telling someone exactly what to do, try inviting them to reflect. You might ask, “What part of your work feels most energizing right now?” Or, “What’s one thing you’d like to try differently?” These kinds of questions spark new ideas and help people discover their own solutions.
Next, spot strengths in action. When you see someone using their strengths, call it out. Maybe they handled a tough client call with patience, or brought creative thinking to a tricky project. Naming those moments helps people recognize what they do well—and it builds real confidence.
Another tip: set short-term goals. Break down big objectives into smaller, manageable steps. And don’t forget to celebrate the wins along the way, no matter how small they seem.
And of course, offer constructive feedback. But do it in a way that taps into the person’s strengths. Instead of focusing only on what went wrong, frame your feedback around how they can use what they’re great at to overcome challenges.
These coaching conversations aren’t just about performance—they’re about helping people grow in ways that really matter to them. When managers show genuine interest in each person’s development, it builds a sense of partnership and trust.
Over time, this approach creates a culture where learning and improvement are part of everyday life. People feel comfortable experimenting, making mistakes, and asking for help. The manager shifts from being a judge to becoming a guide—someone who helps each person find their own unique path to success.
